content_voiceover: This diagram maps out the newer class of drugs called rebalancing agents, which are being developed for hemophilia A and B, especially in patients with inhibitors. The core idea behind rebalancing therapy is that instead of replacing the missing clotting factor, you inhibit one of the body's natural anticoagulant pathways, which shifts the hemostatic balance back toward clot formation. Look at where each agent acts on the cascade. On the left, SerpinPC and VGA039 block the protein C and protein S anticoagulant pathway, which normally degrades factor VIII and factor V, so inhibiting it preserves more active cofactor. On the right, concizumab and marstacimab are monoclonal antibodies that target tissue factor pathway inhibitor, or TFPI, which normally restrains the TF-VIIa complex and factor Xa, so blocking TFPI allows more thrombin generation through the extrinsic pathway. And at the bottom, fitusiran is an siRNA that lowers antithrombin production in the liver, antithrombin being the major natural inhibitor of thrombin and factor Xa, so less antithrombin means more sustained thrombin activity. All three strategies converge on the same goal, more thrombin and more fibrin, without needing to infuse factor VIII or IX directly.
keypoints: Rebalancing agents restore hemostasis by inhibiting natural anticoagulants, not by replacing factor
SerpinPC and VGA039 block the protein C and protein S pathway to preserve factor V and VIII
Concizumab and marstacimab are anti-TFPI antibodies that unleash the TF-VIIa and factor Xa complex
Fitusiran is an siRNA that lowers antithrombin, prolonging thrombin activity
keypoint_voiceover: Know these three targets for boards, TFPI is blocked by concizumab and marstacimab, antithrombin is silenced by fitusiran, and the protein C, protein S pathway is inhibited by SerpinPC and VGA039, all converging to boost thrombin generation.
